The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
The quotient vector space $V/W$ and its canonical projection.

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
The $L^p$ distance for $0 < p < 1$ is a complete translation-invariant metric
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

derivations.claim: The affine map $T:(0,1)\to I$, $T(\xi)=a+\ell\xi$, is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism with derivative $\ell>0$. If $q_1,q_2$ represent the same element of $H_I$, the measurable set $N=\{z\in I:q_1(z)\ne q_2(z)\}$ is null. Apply [F2] to $\mathbf 1_N$ and $T$: $0=\lambda_I(N)=\ell\lambda_{(0,1)}(T^{-1}N)$, so $T^{-1}N$ is null. Therefore the displayed assignment is independent of representatives, and its pointwise formula is linear on representative functions.

For a representative $q$ of an element of $H_I$, apply [F2] to the nonnegative function $z\mapsto |q(z)|^2$. The formula gives $\int_I |q(z)|^2\,dz=\ell\int_0^1|q(a+\ell\xi)|^2\,d\xi=\|U_{a,\ell}[q]\|_{H_0}^2$. The right-hand integral is finite by $q\in H_I$, so the image is in $H_0$, $U_{a,\ell}$ is a well-defined linear map, and the norm is preserved.

The inverse affine map $T^{-1}:I\to(0,1)$ is also a $C^1$ diffeomorphism. The same null-set argument makes $V_{a,\ell}$ independent of the representative, and change of variables for $T^{-1}$, whose derivative is $1/\ell$, gives $\|V_{a,\ell}[g]\|_{H_I}^2=\ell^{-1}\int_I|g((z-a)/\ell)|^2\,dz=\int_0^1|g(\xi)|^2\,d\xi$. Direct substitution gives $V_{a,\ell}U_{a,\ell}[q]=[q]$ and $U_{a,\ell}V_{a,\ell}[g]=[g]$; hence $V_{a,\ell}$ is the inverse and $U_{a,\ell}$ is bijective.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $H=L^2([0,1],\mathcal B,\lambda;\mathbb R)$ be the real Hilbert space of almost-everywhere classes of square-integrable real profiles, with $\langle u,v\rangle_H=\int_0^1u(\xi)v(\xi)\,d\xi$, where $\mathcal B$ is generated by intervals with rational endpoints and $\lambda$ is Lebesgue measure restricted to $\mathcal B$. Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ and $(S,\mathcal S,\nu)$ be probability spaces, let $(\delta_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be independent identically distributed measurable $S$-valued random elements on $\Omega$ with law $\nu$, and let $f:S^{\mathbb N_0}\to H$ be measurable from the product sigma-algebra $\mathcal S^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}$ to the Borel sigma-algebra of $H$. The associated causal profile process is $X_t=f(\delta_t,\delta_{t-1},\ldots)$. Assume $X_0$ is Bochner integrable and has Bochner mean $\mathbb E_BX_0:=\int_\Omega X_0(\omega)\,d\mathbb P(\omega)=0$, with $\mathbb E\|X_0\|_H^2<\infty$. Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice and take an independent product extension carrying the countable replacement-innovation family.

For every $t\in\mathbb Z$, $m\ge1$, and $k\le t-m$, let $\delta'_{t,m,k}$ have law $\nu$, with all these copies mutually independent and independent of the original innovations. Set

$$X_{t,m}=f(\delta_t,\ldots,\delta_{t-m+1},\delta'_{t,m,t-m},\delta'_{t,m,t-m-1},\ldots),\qquad \delta_m=\bigl(\mathbb E\|X_0-X_{0,m}\|_H^2\bigr)^{1/2}.$$

The profile process is $L^2$-$m$-approximable when $\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\delta_m<\infty$. For data $X_1,\ldots,X_n\in H$, $n\ge1$, and an integer block length $1\le b\le n$, moving-block resampling independently draws starts uniformly from $\{1,\ldots,n-b+1\}$, concatenates the corresponding ordered length-$b$ blocks, and truncates the last block to obtain exactly $n$ resampled elements $X_1^*,\ldots,X_n^*$. Define $\bar X_n^*=n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^nX_j^*$, and let $\mathbb E^*$ denote expectation over these draws with the observations fixed. For any bounded real-linear functional $L:H\to\mathbb R$, let $\|L\|=\sup_{\|u\|_H\le1}|L(u)|$; the centered resampled scalar profile summary is $\sqrt n\,L(\bar X_n^*-\mathbb E^*\bar X_n^*)$. This definition specifies the data space and resampling law; it does not assert asymptotic validity.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H=L^2([0,1])$, and let $(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a centered causal Bernoulli shift that is $L^2$-$m$-approximable under [[def-l2-m-approximable-causal-bernoulli-shift]]. Write

$$\delta_m=\bigl(E\|X_0-X_{0,m}\|_H^2\bigr)^{1/2}.$$

By [[lem-independent-tail-replacement-errors-are-monotone]], the summability in the stated process definition implies $m\delta_m\to0$. For each $n$, let $b_n$ be an integer with $b_n\to\infty$ and $b_n/\sqrt n\to0$. For all sufficiently large $n$, these conditions give $1\le b_n\le n$; apply [[alg-moving-block-bootstrap]] to $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ on this admissible tail. All limits below concern that tail. Let $\Gamma$ be the long-run covariance operator from [[thm-hilbert-valued-clt-for-l2-m-approximable-bernoulli-shifts]], and let $\bar X_n^*=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^nX_t^*$. Then

$$\mathcal L^*\!\left(\sqrt n(\bar X_n^*-E^*\bar X_n^*)\right)\Rightarrow\mathcal L(G)\quad\hbox{in probability},$$

and

$$\left\|n\,\operatorname{Cov}^*(\bar X_n^*)-\Gamma\right\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\longrightarrow0\quad\hbox{in probability},$$

where $G$ is the centered $H$-valued Gaussian with covariance $\Gamma$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H=L^2([0,1],dt;\mathbb R)$ and let
$(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a centered, $L^2$-$m$-approximable causal
Bernoulli shift as defined in
[[def-l2-m-approximable-causal-bernoulli-shift]], with Bochner mean
$\mathbb E_BX_0=0$. Let $\Gamma$ be its long-run covariance operator from
[[lem-long-run-covariance-is-trace-class]], and let $G$ be a centered
$H$-valued Gaussian random element with covariance $\Gamma$, whose existence
is given by [[lem-positive-trace-class-covariance-defines-hilbert-gaussian]].
Then, for $S_n=\sum_{t=1}^nX_t$,
$$n^{-1/2}S_n\ \Rightarrow\ G$$
in the weak topology of Borel probability measures on $H$. The covariance
kernel is the $L^2([0,1]^2)$ equivalence class $c$ in the long-run covariance
lemma, and its integral operator is $T_c=\Gamma$. This is a CLT for the
$H$-valued sample sums; it is not a functional CLT for the time-indexed
partial-sum process.

Let $E$ be a separable complete metric space, let $\mathcal D_n$ be the sigma-algebra generated by the observed data at sample size $n$, and let $Z_n^*$ be a bootstrap random element whose remaining randomness is the resampling randomization. Write $\mathcal L^*(Z_n^*)$ for its conditional Borel probability law given $\mathcal D_n$. Supply as part of the data a metric $d_w$ on Borel probability measures on $E$ such that $d_w(\mu_n,\mu)\to0$ exactly when $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ in the sense of [[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]. Assume the displayed metric distance is a measurable real random variable. For a fixed Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $E$, we say that $Z_n^*$ converges conditionally weakly in probability to $\mu$ when

$$d_w\!\left(\mathcal L^*(Z_n^*),\mu\right)\longrightarrow 0\quad\hbox{in probability}.$$

The metric is supplied as a hypothesis; this definition makes no metric-existence assertion. It applies to separable complete metric spaces, including separable Banach spaces, their closed linear subspaces and finite products.

For Borel probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, write $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ if $\int f\,d\mu_n\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function f on S. Continuity is Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form. Such f is Borel measurable (inverse images of open sets are open) and $\int|f|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\mu(S)<\infty$, so the integrals are finite in Integrable real and complex functions, and their integrals. No completeness or coupling is required.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ (The dual space X^* of a normed space and its dual norm). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm (The operator norm as the least bound and as the unit-sphere or unit-ball supremum). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

Let $\mathcal B$ be the Borel sigma-algebra of $[0,1]$, generated by intervals with rational endpoints; let $dt$ be Lebesgue measure restricted to $\mathcal B$, and set $H=L^2([0,1],\mathcal B,dt;\mathbb R)$, with inner product $\langle x,y\rangle_H=\int_0^1x(u)y(u)\,du$. We use the quotient-by-null-functions convention for $L^2$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). The measure space is finite and countably generated, so under Countable Choice $H$ is separable ([[thm-l-p-of-a-sigma-finite-countably-generated-measure-space-is-separable]], [[def-countable-choice]], [[def-separable-space]]); [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]] verifies that this real pairing makes the quotient a Hilbert space.

Let $(S,\mathcal S,\nu)$ be a probability space and $(\delta_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ an independent identically distributed family of $S$-valued random elements with law $\nu$ ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]], [[def-independent-random-elements]]). A **causal Bernoulli shift** with innovation law $\nu$ is a process
$$X_t=f(\delta_t,\delta_{t-1},\delta_{t-2},\ldots),\qquad t\in\mathbb Z,$$
where $f:S^{\mathbb N_0}\to H$ is measurable from the product sigma-algebra $\mathcal S^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}$ to the Borel sigma-algebra of $H$. This product-measurability formulation is meaningful for a merely measurable innovation space $S$.

On an independent product extension, take replacement innovations $\delta'_{t,m,k}$, indexed by $t\in\mathbb Z$, $m\in\mathbb N_0$, and integers $k\le t-m$, all with law $\nu$, mutually independent, and independent of the original innovations. Such a countable family and its product with the original probability space exist under Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]], [[cor-countable-independent-copies-exist]], [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]). For $m\ge1$ define
$$X_{t,m}=f(\delta_t,\ldots,\delta_{t-m+1},\delta'_{t,m,t-m},\delta'_{t,m,t-m-1},\ldots),$$
and define the full replacement $X_{t,0}=f(\delta'_{t,0,t},\delta'_{t,0,t-1},\ldots)$. Each $X_{t,m}$ has the same marginal law as $X_t$; for fixed $m\ge1$ the sequence $(X_{t,m})_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ is strictly stationary and $m$-dependent because its original-innovation windows have length $m$ and its replacement arrays are independent across $t$.

For every fixed $m\ge0$, the joint process $(X_t,X_{t,m})_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ is strictly stationary: shifting all indices relabels a family of mutually independent innovations with the same law and commutes with the defining measurable maps. Consequently $D_{t,m}:=X_t-X_{t,m}$ is stationary and $\|D_{t,m}\|_{L^2(H)}=\delta_m$ for every $t$.

Write $\|X\|_{L^2(H)}=(\mathbb E\|X\|_H^2)^{1/2}$ and
$$\delta_m=\|X_0-X_{0,m}\|_{L^2(H)},\qquad m\ge0.$$
The process is **$L^2$-$m$-approximable** when
$$\mathbb E\|X_0\|_H^2<\infty\qquad\hbox{and}\qquad\sum_{m\ge1}\delta_m<\infty.$$
The same marginal law gives $\delta_0\le2\|X_0\|_{L^2(H)}<\infty$. For a Bochner-integrable $H$-valued random element $Y$, write $\mathbb E_B Y=\int Y\,d\mathbb P$; the moment condition makes $X_t$ and every $X_{t,m}$ Bochner integrable ([[def-bochner-integrable-function]], [[thm-bochner-integrability-criterion]]).

Here **strict stationarity** means invariance of every finite-dimensional law under integer shifts. A process is **$m$-dependent** if, for every $a\in\mathbb Z$, the sigma-algebras generated by $(X_s)_{s\le a}$ and $(X_s)_{s\ge a+m+1}$ are independent ([[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]]). The stated input windows for $X_{t,m}$ are disjoint across these two index ranges, so they satisfy this definition.

Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a
sequence in $H$ whose range $\{x_n : n\in\mathbb N\}$ is dense in $H$
([[def-dense-top]]), and let

$$L_0:=\varnothing,\qquad L_{n+1}:=L_n\cup\Bigl\{\tfrac{v_n}{\|v_n\|}\Bigr\}\ \text{ if }\ v_n:=x_n-\sum_{e\in L_n}\langle x_n,e\rangle e\ne0, \qquad L_{n+1}:=L_n\ \text{ otherwise}.$$

Then $L:=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}L_n$ is a finite or countably infinite orthonormal
set whose closed linear span is $H$; that is, $L$ is an orthonormal basis of $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), and
it is obtained from the given sequence by Gram–Schmidt elimination. The
enumeration of $L$ is the canonical one by the stage at which an element
appears, and no choice principle is used.

Throughout, $H$ and $K$ are real or complex Hilbert spaces with the pairing
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-hilbert-space]]), $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ is a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]) of
operator norm $\|T\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]), and $E$ is a **Hilbert basis**
of $H$, that is, a complete orthonormal subset of $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]).
The basis $E$ is **supplied as data**; the definitions below are stated
relative to it.

**The Hilbert–Schmidt square-sum.** The family $(\|Te\|^2)_{e\in E}$ consists of
nonnegative real numbers and is indexed by the arbitrary set $E$. Its sum is the
supremum of the finite subsums,

$$s_E(T):=\sum_{e\in E}\|Te\|^2:=\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{e\in F}\|Te\|^2 \;:\; F\subseteq E \text{ finite}\Bigr\}\in[0,+\infty],$$

in the finite-subset-supremum convention of
[[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]; the empty finite
subset contributes the empty sum $0$, so the supremum is over a nonempty
set and exists in $[0,+\infty]$. No enumeration, ordering or countability of
$E$ is used or asserted, and no choice is performed: the supremum ranges over
the set of finite subsets of the fixed index set $E$. For finite $E$ the
supremum is the ordinary finite sum over $E$, because all terms are
nonnegative.

**Hilbert–Schmidt relative to a basis.** The operator $T$ is
**Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $E$** when $s_E(T)<+\infty$, that is, when the
finite subsums are bounded above in $\mathbb R$. In that case the
**Hilbert–Schmidt norm of $T$ relative to $E$** is the nonnegative square root

$$\|T\|_{HS,E}:=\Bigl(\sum_{e\in E}\|Te\|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\in[0,+\infty).$$

When $s_E(T)=+\infty$, no Hilbert–Schmidt norm relative to $E$ is defined, and
$T$ is not Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $E$.

**Degenerate and extreme cases.** The zero operator satisfies $s_E(0)=0$ for
every basis $E$, so it is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to every basis with norm
$0$. If $H=\{0\}$ then the empty family is a Hilbert basis of $H$, the only
finite subset is empty, and $s_\varnothing(T)=0$ for the only linear operator
$T:\{0\}\to K$; that operator is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to the empty basis
with norm $0$. If $H$ is finite dimensional and $E$ is finite, $s_E(T)$ is an
ordinary finite sum of the squared norms $\|Te\|^2$, and $T$ is automatically
Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $E$.

**The basis is part of the notation.** The symbol $\|T\|_{HS,E}$ keeps the
basis in the subscript on purpose. Until the next result is proved, the phrase
"$T$ is Hilbert–Schmidt" is never used without a specified Hilbert basis, and
nothing here asserts that a Hilbert basis of $H$ exists: the existence of $E$
is a hypothesis of the definition, and the question of whether the finiteness
of $s_E(T)$ and the value $\|T\|_{HS,E}$ depend on $E$ is taken up in
[[thm-hilbert-schmidt-norm-is-basis-independent]]. In particular this
definition makes no basis-existence claim and no comparison with the operator
norm $\|T\|$; every such statement is proved later, where its own hypotheses
are displayed.

**Notation.** For a finite $F\subseteq E$ we write
$s_F(T):=\sum_{e\in F}\|Te\|^2$ for the finite subsum, so that
$s_E(T)=\sup\{s_F(T):F\subseteq E \text{ finite}\}$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-operator-norm]]), with Hilbert adjoint
$T^*\in\mathcal B(K,H)$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]],
[[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]). Let $E$ be a Hilbert basis of $H$ and $F$ a
Hilbert basis of $K$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), and
let $s_E(T)=\sum_{e\in E}\|Te\|^2$ and $s_F(T^*)=\sum_{f\in F}\|T^*f\|^2$ be the
finite-subset-supremum sums of
[[def-hilbert-schmidt-operator]] and
[[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. Then:

1. **(matrix-coefficient form)** the finite-subset supremum
   $$\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{e\in A}\sum_{f\in B}|\langle Te,f\rangle|^2 \;:\; A\subseteq E,\ B\subseteq F \text{ finite}\Bigr\}$$
   equals $s_E(T)$, and it also equals $s_F(T^*)$;
2. **(basis independence)** $s_E(T)=s_{E'}(T)$ for every Hilbert basis $E'$ of
   $H$, and $s_E(T)=s_F(T^*)$ for every Hilbert basis $F$ of $K$;
3. **(membership and norms)** $T$ is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $E$ if and
   only if it is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to every other Hilbert basis of $H$,
   and then $\|T\|_{HS,E}=\|T\|_{HS,E'}=\|T^*\|_{HS,F}$ for all such bases
   $E,E'$ and every Hilbert basis $F$ of $K$; when the common defining sum is
   $+\infty$, none of these Hilbert–Schmidt norms is defined, and $T$ is
   Hilbert–Schmidt relative to none of the bases.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$, $K$
and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $E$ be a Hilbert basis of $H$
(supplied as data), with $s_E(T)=\sum_{e\in E}\|Te\|^2$ the Hilbert–Schmidt
square-sum and $\|T\|_{HS,E}$ the Hilbert–Schmidt norm of
[[def-hilbert-schmidt-operator]]. Then:

1. if $S,T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ are Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $E$, then so is
   $aS+bT$ for all scalars $a,b$, and
   $$\|aS+bT\|_{HS,E}\le|a|\,\|S\|_{HS,E}+|b|\,\|T\|_{HS,E};$$
2. if $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $E$, then for every
   Hilbert basis $F$ of $K$ the adjoint $T^*$ is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $F$
   and
   $$\|T^*\|_{HS,F}=\|T\|_{HS,E};$$
3. if $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $E$ and
   $A\in\mathcal B(K,L)$, $B\in\mathcal B(H_0,H)$ are bounded with $E_0$ a
   Hilbert basis of $H_0$ and $F$ a supplied Hilbert basis of $K$, then
   $AT\in\mathcal B(H,L)$ is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $E$ and
   $TB\in\mathcal B(H_0,K)$ is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $E_0$, with
   $$\|AT\|_{HS,E}\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_{HS,E},\qquad \|TB\|_{HS,E_0}\le\|T\|_{HS,E}\,\|B\|,$$
   and consequently
   $$\|ATB\|_{HS,E_0}\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_{HS,E}\,\|B\| .$$

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\mathcal B$ be the Borel sigma-algebra of $[0,1]$, generated by intervals with rational endpoints; let $dt$ be Lebesgue measure restricted to $\mathcal B$, and set $H=L^2([0,1],\mathcal B,dt;\mathbb R)$, with inner product $\langle x,y\rangle_H=\int_0^1x(u)y(u)\,du$. We use the quotient-by-null-functions convention for $L^2$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). The measure space is finite and countably generated, so under Countable Choice $H$ is separable ([[thm-l-p-of-a-sigma-finite-countably-generated-measure-space-is-separable]], [[def-countable-choice]], [[def-separable-space]]); [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]] verifies that this real pairing makes the quotient a Hilbert space.

Let $(S,\mathcal S,\nu)$ be a probability space and $(\delta_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ an independent identically distributed family of $S$-valued random elements with law $\nu$ ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]], [[def-independent-random-elements]]). A **causal Bernoulli shift** with innovation law $\nu$ is a process
$$X_t=f(\delta_t,\delta_{t-1},\delta_{t-2},\ldots),\qquad t\in\mathbb Z,$$
where $f:S^{\mathbb N_0}\to H$ is measurable from the product sigma-algebra $\mathcal S^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}$ to the Borel sigma-algebra of $H$. This product-measurability formulation is meaningful for a merely measurable innovation space $S$.

On an independent product extension, take replacement innovations $\delta'_{t,m,k}$, indexed by $t\in\mathbb Z$, $m\in\mathbb N_0$, and integers $k\le t-m$, all with law $\nu$, mutually independent, and independent of the original innovations. Such a countable family and its product with the original probability space exist under Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]], [[cor-countable-independent-copies-exist]], [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]). For $m\ge1$ define
$$X_{t,m}=f(\delta_t,\ldots,\delta_{t-m+1},\delta'_{t,m,t-m},\delta'_{t,m,t-m-1},\ldots),$$
and define the full replacement $X_{t,0}=f(\delta'_{t,0,t},\delta'_{t,0,t-1},\ldots)$. Each $X_{t,m}$ has the same marginal law as $X_t$; for fixed $m\ge1$ the sequence $(X_{t,m})_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ is strictly stationary and $m$-dependent because its original-innovation windows have length $m$ and its replacement arrays are independent across $t$.

For every fixed $m\ge0$, the joint process $(X_t,X_{t,m})_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ is strictly stationary: shifting all indices relabels a family of mutually independent innovations with the same law and commutes with the defining measurable maps. Consequently $D_{t,m}:=X_t-X_{t,m}$ is stationary and $\|D_{t,m}\|_{L^2(H)}=\delta_m$ for every $t$.

Write $\|X\|_{L^2(H)}=(\mathbb E\|X\|_H^2)^{1/2}$ and
$$\delta_m=\|X_0-X_{0,m}\|_{L^2(H)},\qquad m\ge0.$$
The process is **$L^2$-$m$-approximable** when
$$\mathbb E\|X_0\|_H^2<\infty\qquad\hbox{and}\qquad\sum_{m\ge1}\delta_m<\infty.$$
The same marginal law gives $\delta_0\le2\|X_0\|_{L^2(H)}<\infty$. For a Bochner-integrable $H$-valued random element $Y$, write $\mathbb E_B Y=\int Y\,d\mathbb P$; the moment condition makes $X_t$ and every $X_{t,m}$ Bochner integrable ([[def-bochner-integrable-function]], [[thm-bochner-integrability-criterion]]).

Here **strict stationarity** means invariance of every finite-dimensional law under integer shifts. A process is **$m$-dependent** if, for every $a\in\mathbb Z$, the sigma-algebras generated by $(X_s)_{s\le a}$ and $(X_s)_{s\ge a+m+1}$ are independent ([[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]]). The stated input windows for $X_{t,m}$ are disjoint across these two index ranges, so they satisfy this definition.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A strongly measurable function $f:\Omega\to X$ is
**Bochner integrable** if there is a sequence of integrable $X$-valued simple
functions $(s_n)$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega\|f-s_n\|\,d\mu=0.$$

For such a sequence define

$$\int_\Omega f\,d\mu:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega s_n\,d\mu.$$

The displayed norm limit exists: the simple integral inequality gives

$$\left\|\int s_n-\int s_m\right\|\leq\int\|s_n-s_m\|\leq\int\|s_n-f\|+\int\|f-s_m\|,$$

so the simple integrals form a Cauchy sequence, and $X$ is complete. The next
theorem proves that the value is independent of the approximating sequence and
characterizes existence by integrability of $\|f\|$.

For $E\in\mathcal A$, write
$\int_Ef\,d\mu:=\int_\Omega\mathbf1_Ef\,d\mu$ whenever this function is
Bochner integrable.

Let $f:\Omega\to X$ be strongly measurable. Then $f$ is Bochner integrable if
and only if

$$\int_\Omega\|f\|\,d\mu<\infty.$$

Here an a.e.-defined scalar function is integrated through any measurable
representative supplied by the strong simple approximation. Moreover the
Bochner integral is independent of the approximating sequence in its
definition.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be the common probability space for the innovations and their independent replacement family (take a countable independent product extension if needed), and write $\mathbb E$ for expectation under $\mathbb P$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H=L^2([0,1],\mathcal B,\lambda;\mathbb R)$, where $\mathcal B$ is generated by intervals with rational endpoints and $\lambda$ is Lebesgue measure restricted to $\mathcal B$. Let $(S,\mathcal S,\nu)$ be a probability space, let $(\delta_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be independent identically distributed measurable $S$-valued random elements with law $\nu$, and let $f:S^{\mathbb N_0}\to H$ be measurable from the product sigma-algebra $\mathcal S^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}$ to the Borel sigma-algebra of $H$. Set $X_t=f(\delta_t,\delta_{t-1},\ldots)$ and assume its Bochner expectation is zero and $\mathbb E\|X_0\|_H^2<\infty$. For each $t\in\mathbb Z$, $m\ge1$, and $k\le t-m$, let $\delta'_{t,m,k}$ have law $\nu$, with these copies mutually independent and independent of the original innovations, and set $X_{t,m}=f(\delta_t,\ldots,\delta_{t-m+1},\delta'_{t,m,t-m},\delta'_{t,m,t-m-1},\ldots)$. Assume $\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\delta_m<\infty$, where $\delta_m=(\mathbb E\|X_0-X_{0,m}\|_H^2)^{1/2}$. For each $n\ge1$, let the integer block length $b_n$ satisfy $b_n\to\infty$ and $b_n/\sqrt n\to0$; for all sufficiently large $n$, apply moving-block resampling with block length $b_n$ to $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, truncating the last block to exactly $n$ elements. Write $\bar X_n^*=n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^nX_j^*$, and let $\mathbb E^*$ denote expectation over these draws with the observations fixed. For a finite-support $H$-valued resampling random element $Z$, define its conditional covariance operator by

$$\operatorname{Cov}^*(Z):=\mathbb E^*\bigl[(Z-\mathbb E^*Z)\otimes(Z-\mathbb E^*Z)\bigr]\in\mathcal B(H),\qquad (u\otimes v)h:=\langle h,v\rangle_Hu\quad(h,u,v\in H).$$

For a finite-support real-valued resampling random variable $V$, define $\operatorname{Var}^*(V):=\mathbb E^*[(V-\mathbb E^*V)^2]$. Each convergence-in-probability assertion below is with respect to $\mathbb P$.

Write $\mathcal L^*(Z)$ for the law of $Z$ under the same conditional resampling distribution. Let $G$ be the centered $H$-valued Gaussian limit with covariance operator $\Gamma$ supplied by the Hilbert-valued sample-mean CLT for this process. For any bounded real-linear $L:H\to\mathbb R$, set $\|L\|=\sup_{\|u\|_H\le1}|L(u)|$, let $h_L\in H$ be the unique vector satisfying $L(u)=\langle u,h_L\rangle_H$ for every $u\in H$, and define $L^*r=rh_L$. Identify the scalar operator $L\Gamma L^*:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ with its value at $1$. Then
$$\mathcal L^*\!\left(\sqrt n\,L(\bar X_n^*-\mathbb E^*\bar X_n^*)\right)\Rightarrow\mathcal L(LG)\quad\text{in probability},$$
and, with $C_n=n\operatorname{Cov}^*(\bar X_n^*)$,
$$\left|\operatorname{Var}^*\!\left(\sqrt n\,L(\bar X_n^*-\mathbb E^*\bar X_n^*)\right)-L\Gamma L^*\right|\le\|L\|^2\|C_n-\Gamma\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\longrightarrow0\quad\text{in probability}.$$
Here $L\Gamma L^*$ is the variance of the limiting scalar Gaussian. This conclusion concerns bounded linear profile observations under the stated Bernoulli-shift and block-length hypotheses; it makes no claim for nonlinear statistics or for finite-replicate quantile accuracy.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A function $f:\Omega\to X$ is **strongly measurable** (or
**Bochner measurable**) if there are measurable $X$-valued simple functions
$s_n$ and a measurable null set $N$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\|s_n(\omega)-f(\omega)\|=0$$

for every $\omega\in\Omega\setminus N$.

This is a norm-convergence condition. It is not, by definition, merely Borel
measurability of $f$ or measurability of every scalar function $x^*\circ f$.
Changing $f$ on a null set preserves strong measurability: enlarge $N$ by that
null set and retain the same approximants.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

derivations.claim: By [A1] and [F7], the assumed AC yields both DC and Countable Choice, so the product-extension setup in [F1] is available. Use the constant-profile map $\mathcal I:\mathbb R\to H$ defined in the Example. Then $\|\mathcal I(y)\|_H^2=\int_0^1|y|^2\,d\xi=|y|^2$, so $\mathcal I$ is a linear isometry. Since $\mathcal I$ is continuous, $X_t(\omega)=\mathcal I(Y_t(\omega))$ is a measurable causal $H$-valued shift; applying $\mathcal I$ to the same independent replacements gives $X_{t,m}(\omega)=\mathcal I(Y_{t,m}(\omega))$.

The isometry gives $\mathbb E\|X_0\|_H^2=\mathbb E|Y_0|^2$ and $(\mathbb E\|X_0-X_{0,m}\|_H^2)^{1/2}=(\mathbb E|Y_0-Y_{0,m}|^2)^{1/2}$ for every $m$. Apply [F2] to $Y_0$ and the constant random variable $1$ to obtain $\mathbb E|Y_0|\le(\mathbb E|Y_0|^2)^{1/2}<\infty$; hence $\mathbb E\|X_0\|_H<\infty$. By [A1] and [F7], AC supplies Countable Choice, so [F1] gives a countable dense sequence $(h_k)$ in $H$. For each $N$, let $\pi_N(x)$ be a nearest point among $h_1,\ldots,h_N$, resolving ties by the least index. Its finitely many cells are Borel, since they are finite intersections of strict or weak comparisons of continuous distance functions. Thus $\pi_N\circ X_0$ is a measurable finite-valued simple map, and density gives $\pi_N(X_0)\to X_0$ pointwise. By [F6], $X_0$ is strongly measurable, so [F3] gives its Bochner integrability. Since [F3] also gives scalar simple functions $s_j=\sum_k c_{j,k}\mathbf1_{A_{j,k}}$ with $\mathbb E|s_j-Y_0|\to0$, their images satisfy $\mathbb E_B\mathcal I(s_j)=\sum_k\mathbb P(A_{j,k})\mathcal I(c_{j,k})=\mathcal I(\mathbb E s_j)$. The isometry implies $\mathbb E\|\mathcal I(s_j)-X_0\|_H\to0$, so taking the defining integral limits gives $\mathbb E_BX_0=\mathcal I(\mathbb E Y_0)=0$. The profile shift therefore has the required centering and exactly the scalar replacement-error sum.

The functional $L$ is well-defined on almost-everywhere classes, and [F5] gives $|L(v)|\le\|v\|_H\|1\|_H=\|v\|_H$. Since $L(1)=1$ and $\|1\|_H=1$, $\|L\|=1$; also $L(X_t)=\int_0^1Y_t\,d\xi=Y_t$. All hypotheses of [F4] are therefore satisfied, so its conditional bootstrap conclusion applies to this scalar summary.
